_doc: Road-name concordance (DEC-014): for each period road name that a position-ledger claim prints and the gazetteer does not hold, what the period sources (Warren 1868-69, Bachelder 1876, Hopkins 1858, the Official Records) say it is. Written by tools/bt/roadconc/build_concordance.py; do not edit by hand. A name is never aliased to a road by guess: `unresolved` entries say why. `resolved` entries carry a tier (documented: a period map prints the name on the road or an OR report equates the names; inferred: sources of different kinds agree and none contradicts, argument and rejected alternatives written out). The history layer reads only `resolved` entries, through the approach records of data/claim-curation.json that name their id (`concordance`); the geometry used is always a gazetteer line, whose sigma is the gazetteer's.

names.summary: Early, Hays and Blackford place the Heidlersburg road 1.5 to 2 miles north of the town where Bachelder draws Early’s line across the road that he and Warren label Harrisburg Road; Hopkins 1858 runs the road from Heidlersburg into Gettysburg past the Alms Houses on that road; no sheet prints the name Heidlersburg
names.scope: the road from Heidlersburg that enters the field from the north-east: the part inside the loaded ground and the 2.5 km north of it where Early formed his line; farther north the road runs outside the ground and is not needed
names.argument: Early marched down it and formed "across the Heidlersburg road", Hays arrived on it "within a mile and a half" of Gettysburg, Blackford deployed "2 miles from Gettysburg" with his left on the Heidlersburg pike, and Carter reports Doles, on the left of Rodes' line, massing a large force "near the Heidlersburg road" (OR). Bachelder's first-day sheet draws exactly this line (Gordon, Hays, Hoke, Smith, Jones' battalion, "Early's Division") across the road that Bachelder and Warren both label HARRISBURG ROAD, 2.4 to 2.6 km north of the borough centre (1.5 miles), and that road runs from there to the borough past the County Almshouse. Hopkins 1858 draws the road from Heidlersburg running south-west to Gettysburg and entering the borough past the "Alms Houses" on its drawn line; Warren shows the almshouse on the same road. Ewell's sentence names the Middletown road and the Heidlersburg road as two different roads in one breath, and Schurz (Eleventh Corps, whose right stood astride the Harrisburg road) feared the enemy advancing "by the Heidlersburg road" against his right. No source prints "Heidlersburg" on a road of the sheets; the identity rests on the agreement of the OR distances and positions with the drawn road, so the tier is inferred, not documented.

names.summary: Rodes puts Doles on the plain between the Middletown road and the foot of Oak Ridge, apart from the Mummasburg road that crosses the ridge; Bachelder draws Doles’s line across the road he labels Newville Road, which Warren labels Carlisle Road; no sheet prints the name Middletown road
names.scope: the road by which Rodes' division came down to the field from Middletown (Biglerville): the part inside the loaded ground and the 3 km north of it; the roads layer names it Carlisle Road, Warren labels it CARLISLE ROAD near the borough and NEWVILLE ROAD from the farm of W. Ross northward, Bachelder labels it NEWVILLE ROAD
names.argument: Rodes names two roads in one report: the Mummasburg road, "which crossed the ridge at the base of the hill I held" (Oak Hill), and the Middletown road, whose "open plain between the Middletown road and the foot of the ridge" Doles' brigade occupied. A road with a plain between it and the foot of Oak Ridge is the road east of the ridge, which on both sheets is the road labelled CARLISLE ROAD / NEWVILLE ROAD; the Mummasburg road is the one that crosses the ridge, so the Middletown road is not the Mummasburg road. Bachelder draws Doles' line (DOLES GA., 1 P.M.) across the road he labels NEWVILLE ROAD. Schurz writes of "the Middletown and Mummasburg roads" as two roads at the Eleventh Corps' right, west of which his division held the ground. Ewell and Early put Rodes on a different road from Early's Heidlersburg road (RC-01), and Lee says Rodes "arrived by the Middletown road". The roads that are left, the Harrisburg Road (Early's) and the Mummasburg Road (named separately), are excluded by those reports; the Table Rock Road joins this road 1.8 km north of the borough, north of the loaded ground. No sheet prints "Middletown" on the road and no report says "Carlisle road" for Rodes; the identity is by elimination and by the position of Doles' line, so the tier is inferred. Hopkins 1858 shows the village of Middletown about 11 km north of the borough; it was not used for geometry or for the identity.

names.summary: in Kershaw’s own march from Fayetteville the road occupied by Anderson’s division and the Gettysburg road are one road; Hill puts Fayetteville on the road from Chambersburg to Gettysburg and Wright puts Anderson’s division on the turnpike; this passage only
names.scope: ONE PASSAGE ONLY: Kershaw's march of 1 July, report OR27-2-R432 p. 366, claim PD-1c-mclaws-kershaw-02. The phrase "the Gettysburg road" is not a name: in other reports it is the road to Gettysburg from wherever the writer came (RC-04)
names.argument: Kershaw marched to Fayetteville on 30 June; on 1 July "Anderson's and Johnson's divisions and General Ewell's wagon train occupied the road until 4 p. m., when we marched to a point on the Gettysburg road, some 2 miles from that place". It is one march on one road from Fayetteville to the point 2 miles from Gettysburg: "the road" that Anderson's division (Third Corps) had occupied is, in Hill's report, "the road from Chambersburg to Gettysburg, near the village of Fayetteville", and Wright's report of Anderson's division prints the march "along the turnpike in the direction of Gettysburg" (AP-32); the roads layer and Warren (CHAMBERSBURG ... PIKE) name that road the Chambersburg Pike. The step "the road" to "the Gettysburg road" inside one sentence of Kershaw is the only link not printed, so the tier is inferred. It does not extend to the other brigades of McLaws' division (their claims print no road).

names.reason: the phrase is not a name of a road: each writer means the road by which his own column came to Gettysburg (the Second Corps from Taneytown, the Eleventh from Emmitsburg, Kershaw from Fayetteville), and two or more roads of the gazetteer could carry it. No sheet and no report equates it with one road for these passages. The claims keep their place on the cards; none is placed by it.

names.period_name: the road from Scotland to Gettysburg (Johnson's division)
variants: the road from Scotland to Gettysburg
the road west of the mountains
names.reason: Scotland lies in Franklin County and on the Cumberland Valley line (Couch: "Scotland Bridge, 6 miles this side of Chambersburg", OR27-3-D1142 p. 548). Hopkins 1858 covers Adams County only and the Warren sheet ends about 5 km west of the borough, so no period map in the repository shows Scotland or the road from it. The reports say that Johnson "countermarched my division to Greenville, thence eastwardly, via Scotland, to Gettysburg" (Johnson), "marched from Carlisle by the road west of the mountains" (Lee) and that his division "came into the road from Shippensburg" (Longstreet, who does not name the road); none says which road it was on from the mountain to the field. To say the Chambersburg Pike would be a guess from the geography; the OR Atlas plates are not yet acquired (library/status.json). The 17 leaf units of Johnson's division stay an open gap.

names.argument: Johnson and Steuart say that on the night of 1 July the division moved "along the Gettysburg and York Railroad" to the north-east of the town and formed there; Steuart "marched through a part of the town and along the York railroad". Both describe a move inside the field after the unit reached it by another road, so the name gives no road of approach even though it can be placed. The name is not a gazetteer road and no approach record rests on it.

names.period_name: the route by Horner's Mill (Eleventh Corps)
names.reason: a route named by a mill, not a road. Howard says the Second and Third Divisions took it (13 miles against 10 to 11 by the direct road), his dispatch of 1 July says it was chosen 'to relieve the direct road' and that the corps would encamp 'near J. Wintz's place, near the cross-roads, about 3 miles this side of Gettysburg'; Schurz passed Horner's Mills at 10.30. Hopkins 1858 prints Horner's mill and the Horner farms about 8 km south of the borough, near Rock Creek, but no source names the roads of the route, and where it met the road layer (the Emmitsburg road at the cross-roads, or another) is not stated. No road is traced from the map for it: the route would have to be invented between the mill and the cross-roads. The leaf units of the Eleventh Corps's Second and Third Divisions and artillery stay an open gap.
